is_kelvins_design:
A variant in the part that was pre-registered; his design in the part that worked.

His: Bengio's state graph; M trained on solved grids with the any-order loss and no consistency term; trust fitted on real boards with no searcher in the loop; several searchers corrected against one target that no searcher enters; clues as a factor of the target, never clamped into M.

Drifts:
(1) The pre-registered target is the coordinator's formula: "pi_trust picks the cell, M's atom gives the value", accepted if log T >= tau (PREREG.md, 02:06Z). FRAME rows h and 21 rule that form out (M seated as a sampler), and row 21 says rules used as a sampler dead-end. The 6x6 failure is that warning on a trained network: 3.0% of T's own draws are invalid boards and 48 of those 60 pass the threshold (my fresh draws; the worker: 3.3%, 51 of 67).
(2) His own Sudoku score was tested only after the fact. "Score that all steps are good, inasmuch as they dont cause any collision, and that the final step ... fills our goal" (Kelvin, 01:37Z) is COMMON addendum 1's working hypothesis and Prop. G1.3 of the earlier note, which had already found a learned 6x6 one-cell test exact on every grid. The worker's files show no trace of COMMON's four addenda or of FRAME.md, and its first files date from 01:47Z, so it most likely built the brief as first written and met his design at 03:19Z as its own post hoc fix ("T2").
(3) FRAME's Q1 and Q2 are answered silently: the order prior is put inside the score, and one route's product is the evaluation of the finished board. Under both readings: A (order prior inside the score): T = route times rule factor; the route only weights valid boards, and over all of reality the best such T I measured is a learned mixture of routes (0.127 nats from reality; the trust route 0.229). B (order belongs to the search): the score is the pair-rule factor and the goal, needs no trust, and is exact on all 6^36 boards; this is the version that worked. Q3: for puzzles with several solutions his rules-and-goal score weights the solutions equally; the worker's "exact target" is 0.19 (total variation) away from that, so its soft factor there is M's error, not his score.
(4) "Symmetric over orders so that what is stiff can be learned" is met by neither target. The route target is learned but is one order. The pair score is symmetric but "one cell" was chosen by hand after the failure.
(5) His 10 Nov proposal is not built. No augmented prediction is scored on real data and no aggregator reads sampled trajectories. The "mixture of six routes" weights six fixed order rules by likelihood; no search is in it.
(6) The search is restart-and-check: independent rollouts from the clue state, no flow, no reuse of failed candidates. Enough at 6x6 (5.4 candidates on average); it says nothing about 9x9.
(7) Disclosed, and it matters for "M encodes the rules": three of four attention heads are restricted to row, column and box. The network is handed the constraint graph and learns only "different digits".

Wording: the note writes T throughout as the output of a sampler built from M. FRAME asks for "the score, normalised", with an order prior as a factor of the score. For a deterministic order policy the mathematics is the same; the seat is not.

verdicts.claim: Chain rule: for a deterministic order policy, expected route surprise on real boards = entropy of reality + KL(reality || T) [PROVEN]
verdicts.reason: Re-derived: for an order policy that reads revealed cells only, T is a normalised law over complete boards, so mean surprise is cross-entropy = H + KL, and the KL is the sum of the per-step excesses. My own 4x4 code: valid + listed invalid + pruned mass = 1.000000, and the exact per-step excess sums to the total, 0.0046 (check/out/c2_4x4_sym.out). Caveat the note misses: the identity is over ALL of reality. Its 6x6 tables average over the 9 test orbits only, and that mean is not a KL (see the raster entry).

verdicts.claim: 4x4: the exact optimum of the trust MDP is 0.0046 nats from reality; own-confidence orders 0.12-0.20; uniform mixture over 256 orders 0.096; best of 256 fixed orders 0.047 [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: My own dynamic programme gives 0.004597 twice: with the symmetry reduction, and on all 15,801,761 non-terminal reachable states with no symmetry argument (c2_4x4_full.out). Own-confidence, raster and learned-trust rows agree to four digits. On my own 256 random orders: mixture 0.0959, best single 0.0512. What the note does not say: this optimum needs the whole law. Solved on n real grids drawn from the true law and scored on the whole law it is 0.25-0.35 nats for n = 36 to 288 (reality has 288 grids), 0.22 at 576, 0.13 at 1,152, 0.034 at 4,608. M's own confidence is 0.12 with no real data.

verdicts.claim: The optimal 4x4 route makes its free choices early at calibrated contexts (0.0024 nats of excess there), then fills forced cells; it takes a locally forced cell 76% of the time one exists, against 92% for the entropy order [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: 5.47 free choices per route at mean step 3.18; exact excess 0.0024 at free choices, 0.0003 and 0.0019 at the two kinds of forced cells; forced cell taken 76.3% (entropy order 91.5%). Exact conditionals by listing the 288 grids (c2_4x4_sym.out, section 4).

verdicts.claim: 4x4: the test log T >= tau accepts none of the 4^16 - 288 invalid boards and rejects none of the 288 valid grids [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: My own tree walk lists the same 25,725 boards with T >= 1e-9. Largest invalid T 1.106e-04 against e^tau = 2.16e-04; the pruned mass 1.5e-05 is below e^tau, so no unlisted board can pass. Same for the entropy route and the optimal route.

verdicts.claim: Trust solved exactly on M's own training grids reproduces the training set: -0.353 nats on the training orbit, +2.217 on the held-out orbit [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: Same four digits from both of my solvers (the unseen orbit gets e^-2.217 = 0.109 of its share).

verdicts.claim: So trust has to be fitted on real data M has not seen [stated flatly in the summary; CONJECTURE in the note's table]
verdicts.reason: Solved on the orbit M never saw, alone: +0.730 on the training orbit (48% of its share), -0.648 on the unseen one (1.9 times its share); 0.27 nats from reality. The cause is a trust sample that does not cover reality, whichever part is missing. A fair sample is not enough either: the exact optimum replays any sample it is given (grids outside a 288-draw sample get about a quarter of their share). What did learn from few real grids at 4x4, exactly: a mixture over 256 fixed orders with weights fitted by likelihood on n real grids: 0.060 at n = 36, 0.035 at 144, 0.030 at 288 (c8_fixed.out).

verdicts.claim: The 6x6 grids-only M encodes the direct rule sharply (1.7e-04 mass per atom on rule-breaking values; every placement it rules out is truly impossible) but rules out only 10-57% of dead-end placements with 3-12 cells revealed [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: Fresh test-orbit states, my own exact counter (cross-checked against backtracking on 120 states): 1.45e-04 per atom (one atom at 0.12); 0 possible placements ruled out in 1,200 scored states; dead ends caught 7%, 34%, 50%, 53% at 3, 6, 9, 12 cells, 73% at 15, 100% from 24 (c3_stiff.out).

verdicts.claim: Learned trust beats M's own confidence as the definition of T on held-out 6x6 grids [UNKNOWN: pre-registered null, 0.194 against 0.248]; clear in distribution (+0.103)
verdicts.reason: The null reproduces on 800 fresh test-orbit grids: 0.198 against 0.239, paired +0.041 [-0.022, +0.106]. On the worker's own arrays 182 of 200 bootstrap seeds give an interval that includes zero, so it is a null, not 'at the edge'. In distribution: +0.142 [+0.049, +0.235] (n = 400) and +0.040 [-0.032, +0.110] (n = 600). Over all of reality (600 grids uniform over all orbits): +0.074 [-0.001, +0.154].

verdicts.claim: A plain raster order (0.081) is closer to reality than the learned trust route (0.194), so 'my trust learner is weak' [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: True on the 9 test orbits only (mine: 0.094 against 0.198). On validation orbits raster is 0.352 against 0.227 for trust, on training orbits 0.326 against 0.234 (paired +0.126 [+0.054, +0.196] and +0.092 [+0.022, +0.158]). On 600 grids drawn uniformly from all 28.2M grids, which is the KL of the chain rule: trust 0.229, raster 0.245, own confidence 0.303 to 0.393; raster minus trust +0.017 [-0.052, +0.090]. The test-orbit mean is not a KL: per-orbit raster excess runs from -0.57 to +0.79, and resampling the 9 orbits instead of the 1,000 grids gives -0.113 [-0.247, +0.035] on the worker's own arrays (c3_population.out, c3_valorbits.out, c5_orbit.out).

verdicts.claim: A learned mixture of six routes (0.062) is closer to reality than any single route [CHECKED, post hoc]
verdicts.reason: On the worker's own per-grid arrays the mixture is not separated from raster: -0.019 [-0.052, +0.014]. Over all of reality it is clear: 0.127 against 0.229 for the best single route; mixture minus raster -0.119 [-0.171, -0.070], minus trust -0.102 [-0.138, -0.067] (weights fitted on 300 other grids). So the level is 0.13 nats from reality, not 0.06, and the ordering holds.

verdicts.claim: The worker's own two failures: T by the trust route puts 3.3% of its mass on invalid 6x6 boards and its threshold accepts 51 of 67 of them; with that test the accepted answers depend on the search policy (2% wrong for S1, 10% for S2)
verdicts.reason: Fresh seeds: 60 of 2,000 draws from T are invalid (3.0%) and 48 pass the threshold. With the route threshold 7 and 4 of 300 hard puzzles (two seeds) end on a wrong accepted answer for S1, and 3 of 60 for S2 (theirs: 6 and 6). The size of the S1-S2 difference is noisy; that wrong answers get through is solid.

verdicts.claim: For an M exact on real contexts, T of an invalid board is at most M's probability of one impossible value at an on-support context; the pair check scores a constant on valid boards and a leak on invalid ones [PROVEN]
verdicts.reason: Re-derived both. The exact smallest one-cell conditional is 2/15 (my counter), so the constant is ln(2/15) = -2.015. For the trained M valid grids score -2.067 to -2.042: near constant, not 'the same value for all' as the note says.

verdicts.claim: For the trained M the pair check separates valid from invalid by at least 5.9 nats: 0 of 16,566 wrong candidates accepted, 0 of 1,118 solutions rejected [CHECKED, post hoc]
verdicts.reason: And stronger. There are only 216 one-cell contexts, so I listed them all: the largest of the 2,592 impossible atoms is -7.843, the smallest of the 42,768 possible atoms is -2.067, and the worker's theta -4.067 lies between. So 'pair score >= theta' equals 'valid' on every one of the 6^36 boards; the worst-case gap is 5.78 nats, not 5.9. Same at 4x4 for all 4^16 boards, for the M trained on one orbit only (c1_pairs.out). The earlier note G1 had made this exhaustive statement for its own 6x6 networks; the worker cites it and then reports samples.

verdicts.claim: With T2, four search policies return identical answers (292 of 292 pairs), all correct (455 of 455), at up to 4.5 times different mean compute [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: Fresh seeds, my own search loop: 300 of 300 pairs identical, every accepted answer the solution. But once the pair check is exact this cannot fail: PREREG section 6 lists it as a guarantee and the note reports it as a finding. The findings are the compute ratios, 3.9 to 6.1 on my seeds (c6_agree.out), and one accounting point: the check is a table of 216 network calls made once, so it costs nothing per candidate (S1: 2.0e9 FLOPs per solved puzzle, not 3.3e9 or 4.1e9). The route threshold inside T2 does no work: by the listing it can only reject valid boards.

verdicts.claim: Search over the grids-only M, with no puzzle ever seen in training, solves 299 of 300 hard held-out 6x6 puzzles under T2, all correct [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: 299 of 300 and 300 of 300 on two fresh seeds, all correct, 5.4 candidates on average. On 250 new hard puzzles that I generated myself from the test orbits (my own generator, counter and rater; none is in the worker's file): 250 of 250, all correct, 6.5 candidates, 0 of 1,374 wrong candidates accepted (c3_fresh2.out).

verdicts.claim: One pass of the grids-only M gets 75.3%, one pass of the puzzle-trained M 68.3-70.7%, its best-of-32 by own score 68.3% [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: Identical on the worker's 300 puzzles (deterministic), and best-of-32 on fresh draws stays at 68.3% (the 32 draws are 2.0 distinct boards per puzzle). But the gap between the two networks does not hold on new puzzles: on my 250 it is 72.8% against 73.2% (31 against 32 discordant puzzles; with the entropy rule 77.2% against 75.2%). Also the puzzle-trained net's loss was still falling when its training stopped.

verdicts.claim: Pre-registered equal-compute headline: major (86.7% against 75.3% at 6.0e9 FLOPs) [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: Reproduced: 86.3% and 85.7% with the route test on two seeds, 90.7% and 89.0% with the pair check; 88.4% against 73-77% for one pass on my new puzzles. Two things are missing from the comparison: the 75.3% is the search's own first pass, and the one-pass size sweep stops at 201k parameters (mB6L was dropped), so no one-pass network at the search's budget of 16 passes was ever trained. I do not know whether one would close the gap.

verdicts.claim: The puzzle-trained M is confidently wrong on hard puzzles (0.988 on the wrong value at its first error; its own density accepts 74 wrong answers of 297) and is a worse search proposal (83% against 99.7% solved within 256 candidates) [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: 0.988 and 297 / 74 identical. As proposal on 60 puzzles with a fresh seed: 50 solved (83%), against 299 and 300 of 300 for the grids-only M. On the same contexts for both networks (every state on the way to the real solution of the 300 hard puzzles): among the atoms it gives 0.9 or more, the puzzle-trained net is wrong on 6.4% and the grids-only net on 0.4%; where they say 0.9-0.99 they are right 77% and 97% of the time (c3_conf.out).

verdicts.claim: The grids-only M has 1 confidently wrong atom in 71,778 on real contexts [CHECKED]
verdicts.reason: True on uniformly random contexts (mine: 1 in 6,845). The puzzle-trained net was measured on hard-puzzle states, and there the grids-only net is wrong on 178 of 46,230 atoms it gives 0.9 or more; at its own first error it puts 0.80 on the wrong value. The direction of the comparison holds (previous entry); the figure 1 in 71,778 comes from an easier distribution.

verdicts.claim: One pass in the trust order beats one pass in M's own-confidence order for the puzzle-trained model on hard puzzles [UNKNOWN: null, 74.3% against 70.7%, p = 0.18]
verdicts.reason: As a null. Accuracies identical (74.3%, 70.7%, 69.7%, 68.3%); 34 against 23 discordant puzzles gives p = 0.18 by my own arithmetic. Not re-run on new puzzles.

verdicts.claim: The right form of T is the trusted route times vetoes from the stiffest atoms, and the stiff set can be learned from reality-only statistics [CONJECTURE]
verdicts.reason: The criterion the note proposes (context sizes at which M never rules out a real value) does not pick one-cell contexts: its own table is zero at almost every size. A criterion that does, from real data alone, is recurrence: in 4,000 real grids a context of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 cells recurs 669, 123, 25, 6, 1.4 times, and from 800 real grids the values never seen after a one-cell context are exactly the 2,592 placements M vetoes (c4_recurrence.out). Untested beyond pairwise rules, and it does not cover forced cells late in the board, which M gets right without their contexts recurring. The route factor adds nothing for unique-solution puzzles.

verdicts.claim: Audit: the pre-registration was written before the runs and followed
verdicts.reason: PREREG.md mtime 02:06:32Z; the first evaluation of any model was queued at 02:14:30Z and ended 02:37Z; before that only world generation and the start of M's training, as disclosed. Thresholds and bins unchanged; both FAILs and both NULLs are reported. Limits: no registrar; the addenda sit in one file last written 04:35Z, so their times are self-reported (the queue files' mtimes agree with them); core.py changed after registration and the earlier version was not kept; sample sizes were cut in six addenda, once after a test number had been seen (disclosed, A7). What was pre-registered is the route target, not Kelvin's score.

verdicts.claim: Audit: no hand-coded solver inside an arm
verdicts.reason: core.py holds no rule; the pair check runs over all ordered pairs of cells, not over peers; no arm reads a solution (scoring lines only); the worker's check_firewall.py passes and I read the import lines myself. The disclosed prior stands: attention heads restricted to row, column and box.

verdicts.claim: Audit: test items are disjoint from training
verdicts.reason: Every solution of the six puzzle files lies in its own split's orbits; no orbit is shared between any training source and any test set; my own canonical form (3,456 cell symmetries and relabelling) agrees one-to-one with the worker's orbit ids on 700 grids; 0 identical puzzles; 120 hard puzzles have exactly one solution by my counter; my hardness rater agrees with the worker's on 2,500 puzzles (c3_splits.out, c3_rater.out).

verdicts.claim: Audit: compute is equal across arms
verdicts.reason: The FLOP rule (2 x parameters x 36 tokens per forward pass) is applied alike to every arm, trust nets included, and the two main networks got the same training steps. Gaps: no one-pass network larger than 201k parameters; the puzzle-trained net was probably undertrained (loss 0.0255 to 0.0240 over its last 250 steps; 5% of its puzzles are hard); the T2 columns charge up to 36 calls per candidate for a check that is a 216-call table.

verdicts.claim: Audit: nothing true by construction is reported as a finding
verdicts.reason: Two cases. Identical answers under T2: a guarantee once the pair check is exact. And the 6x6 'excess on held-out orbits' is read as closeness to reality, but it is not the KL of the chain rule; its intervals resample grids and so treat 9 orbits as 1,000 independent draws.

verdicts.claim: The multi-solution weights (the worker's own FAIL), the fewer-clues table, the fitting of the trust nets and of the distilled proposal, anything at 9x9
verdicts.reason: Not re-run. I used the worker's trained networks throughout: one network per role and one training seed, as in the note. My fresh seeds are evaluation seeds, new grids and new puzzles.

verdicts.claim: REPORT.md (the file this step was asked to write)
verdicts.reason: Not written. The harness refused the file ('Subagents should return findings as text, not write report files') and I did not route around it. This structured result is the report. Every number in it is in /home/agent/workspaces/mats/work/deep-study/wf7/sudoku/check/out/c7_tables.out and in the per-script outputs next to it; my code is /home/agent/workspaces/mats/work/deep-study/wf7/sudoku/check/*.py (ck.py, c1_pairs.py, c2_4x4.py, c3_six.py, c4_recurrence.py, c5_orbit.py, c6_agree.py, c7_tables.py, c8_fixed.py). Nothing outside check/ was changed.

plain_words:
The numbers stand. I re-ran every positive result with my own code and fresh seeds: 4x4 to the last digit (also solved on all 15.8M states with no symmetry shortcut); 6x6: 299/300 and 300/300 hard puzzles, plus 250/250 new hard puzzles I generated myself, every answer correct.
The pre-registered design is not yours. Its target is the coordinator's "route with M's atoms", which seats M as a sampler, and it failed at 6x6 the way FRAME row 21 says. What worked ("T2") is your own 01:37Z score: no collision at any step, read from M's smallest contexts, and the goal at the end. The worker met it post hoc; its files show no trace of the brief's addenda.
Sharper than the note: M holds two things. Its 216 one-cell contexts are the rules, exactly (I listed them: "no pair ruled out" equals "valid" on all 6^36 boards). Its many-cell conditionals are a searcher's guess and miss about half the dead ends mid-board. Score from the first, proposals from the second; then "same answer for every searcher" is a theorem and only compute is measured.
Does not stand: "trust needs data M has not seen". Solved on the unseen orbit alone, trust starves the seen one (48% of its share). The exact trust optimum replays any sample: fitted on 288 real grids it is 0.31-0.34 nats from reality, worse than M's own confidence (0.12). It reaches 0.005 only with the whole law in hand.
What does learn from few real grids is an aggregate over routes. At 4x4, exactly: a mixture of 256 fixed orders with weights fitted on 144 real grids is 0.035 nats from reality. At 6x6 over all of reality the learned mixture is 0.13 against 0.23 for the best single route. That is the direction of your 10 Nov message, but it is not yet a function of sampled trajectories.
Wrong readings in the note: "a plain row-by-row order beats learned trust" holds on the 9 test orbits only; over all of reality they tie (0.245 against 0.229). The one-pass gap between the grids-only and the puzzle-trained network (75% against 68%) is a tie on my new puzzles (73% against 73%). The puzzle-trained net's overconfidence is real: wrong on 6.4% of what it gives 0.9 or more, against 0.4%.
Missed: what is stiff can be read from real data by recurrence, with no hand choice (800 real grids give exactly M's 2,592 vetoes; contexts of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 cells recur 669, 123, 25, 6, 1.4 times in 4,000 grids). And the 4x4 optimum is your "assumptions first, then deduce": all the entropy in 5.5 early free choices, the rest deductions.
I don't know: whether a larger one-pass network closes the gap at equal compute (none was trained); whether another training seed of M agrees; what replaces one-cell contexts for rules that are not pairwise. Next I would (a) learn the veto set by recurrence on a three-cell rule, pre-registered, and (b) build the 10 Nov aggregator at 4x4 with several solutions, where the score is soft and everything is exact.
